name: Sublunary versus supralunary cosmology (the fifth element)
plain_explanation: Everything below the moon (the sublunary sphere) is made of the four familiar elements -- earth, water, air, fire -- and is subject to generation and decay; everything from the moon outward is made of a fifth, perfect element ('quintessence') that never comes into being or passes away, and whose natural motion is circular rather than the up-and-down motion of the terrestrial elements.
precise_definition: The cosmology of On the Heavens, dividing the universe into a corruptible sublunary region composed of the four terrestrial elements (whose natural motions are rectilinear: fire and air upward, earth and water downward, in proportion to relative 'lightness' and 'heaviness') and an eternal, incorruptible supralunary region composed of a fifth element, whose only natural motion is perfect circular rotation, carrying the stars and planets on attached spheres.
why_it_mattered: This cosmology dominated Western astronomy and physics until Galileo, and directly generated the later terms 'quintessence' and 'sublunary'; Russell notes its poetic afterlife in Dante's Paradiso.
historical_origin: Set out in On the Heavens as the direct continuation of the Physics's argument for an unmoved mover causing circular motion.
examples: Comets were classified as sublunary (destructible) phenomena on this theory, since they appear and disappear -- a classification later overturned when seventeenth-century astronomers showed comets orbit the sun and are rarely as near as the moon.
objections: Russell: 'nothing in the visible world is exempt from change and decay'; stars and the sun are born from nebulae and eventually explode or die of cold, so the doctrine of eternal, incorruptible heavenly bodies has had to be abandoned entirely, a view Russell calls 'a product of the pagan worship of sun and moon and planets.'
competing_positions: Modern astrophysics, in which all matter, terrestrial and celestial, is subject to the same physical laws and processes of change.
influence_on_later_thinkers: Directly shaped medieval astronomy and cosmology, and the associated vocabulary ('quintessence,' 'sublunary') long outlived the theory itself.
connection_to_politics_or_religion: Russell traces the belief in eternal, incorruptible heavenly bodies to the pagan worship of the sun, moon, and planets as gods.
